title: Let my people go (Exodus 5–10)
hookLine: bricks without straw, then plagues against a hardened heart
carry: this is the finger of God

cards: Moses and Aaron walk into Pharaoh's court and say four words: "Let my people go." Enslaved people in America would later sing them in the spiritual Go Down, Moses.
Pharaoh's answer is a shrug: who is this Lord, that I should listen to him? I don't know him. Then he does something any overworked employee would recognize.
He raises the quota. Same number of bricks every day, he orders, but no more straw. Go find your own.

teach.b: First, the bricks. The Hebrews scatter across Egypt gathering stubble, and they can't make the count. The Egyptian taskmasters beat the Hebrew foremen.

The foremen go to Pharaoh and get nowhere, and on the way out they turn on Moses: you've made us stink in Pharaoh's eyes. And Moses turns to God: why did you ever send me? Things got worse the moment I spoke.

teach.h: NINE PLAGUES, AND THE FINGER OF GOD.
teach.b: Second, the plagues. Blood in the Nile. Frogs.
Gnats. Flies. Sickness on the cattle.
Then darkness so thick it can be felt. Nine in these chapters; the tenth comes tomorrow. Pharaoh's magicians copy the first ones, then give up at the gnats and tell him: this is the finger of God.
Third, the hard heart. Again and again Pharaoh promises to let the people go, then changes his mind when the trouble lifts.
Sometimes the text says Pharaoh hardened his own heart; elsewhere, that God hardened it. Readers have long wrestled with that.

Saint Augustine and Saint Thomas Aquinas taught that God doesn't put evil into anyone; when God is said to harden a heart, God withholds grace from someone who has already chosen to refuse it. Fourth, the cry.
This is a story about bricks and wages and bodies, not only souls.
The Catechism lists cheating workers of their wages among the sins that cry out to heaven, and Pope Leo the Thirteenth wrote a whole letter, Rerum Novarum, on the rights of workers.
That teaching leans on stories like this one: God hearing the cry of people forced to work without straw.

how: Catholic social teaching, beginning with Pope Leo XIII's letter Rerum Novarum in 1891, defends workers' right to a just wage, and the Catechism lists defrauding laborers of their wages among the sins that cry to heaven.

games.q: you're Pharaoh. Moses and Aaron just told you their God says let my people go. what's your move?
o: let them go for a few days to worship.
keep the brick quota and take away their straw.
games.why: he doesn't argue. he makes the work harder: same number of bricks, and they gather their own straw.

practice: Think of the people whose work you depend on and rarely see: whoever picked the fruit in your kitchen, sewed the shirt you're wearing, cleans the building you work in, drives the truck with your packages; some are paid fairly, and some are making bricks without straw.
If you pray, pray for them by name or by work, with Moses's words, let my people go; if you don't, hold them in mind with respect.

wordCard.voice: Rerum Novarum, the letter on workers' rights by Pope Leo the Thirteenth, leaning on this very story: bricks without straw, and a cry God hears. Today's word.
